title: Checkpoint: How Chance Works
objective: After this level you can work out simple chances with dice and coins, and explain why luck does not "even out" in the short run.
summary: Count equally likely outcomes, multiply independent chances, and take "none" from 1 for "at least one". Luck doesn't even out: each try starts fresh and early luck is swamped.

cards.headline: Could you have saved the Monte Carlo crowd a fortune?
cards.body: Chapter 3 has handed you a small kit for reasoning about chance. This checkpoint puts it together and answers the question behind the whole chapter: does luck even out?

cards.headline: Three tools for any chance question
cards.body: Count: when outcomes are equally likely, divide the ones you want by all of them (7 is 6 of the 36 throws of two dice). Multiply: for independent events, the chance of both is the product (double 6 is 1/6 × 1/6). Flip: for "at least one", find the chance of none and take it from 1 (a six in four rolls, about 52%).

cards.headline: What luck does, and doesn't do

items.label: Many tries
points: The share settles near the chance
Early luck is swamped, not repaid

cards.headline: Surprises are often counting mistakes
cards.body: Galileo's dice and the birthday problem fool intuition the same way: we count the wrong thing. Count throws, not totals, and three dice make 10 more often than 9. Count pairs, not people, and 23 people make 253 pairs, enough for a 50.7% chance of a shared birthday. When a chance surprises you, check what's being counted.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 complete
learned: How to work out a chance by counting, multiplying, or taking the chance of none away from 1.
Why a coin that landed heads five times is still 50/50, and where the gambler's fallacy goes wrong.
Why luck doesn't even out in the short run, and why real randomness is full of streaks.
Why 23 people are enough for a better than even chance of a shared birthday.

questions.prompt: Match each chance tool with when to use it.
questions.explanation: Count when outcomes are equally likely, multiply for independent events, and flip (find the chance of none, take it from 1) for "at least one".

questions.prompt: After ten heads in a row, a friend says tails is due "because luck evens out". How does the chapter answer that?

options.label: Tails is due, but only after twenty more flips
options.rationale: No number of flips makes tails due.

options.label: Luck evens out exactly, so the count will balance
options.rationale: The count need not balance: Kerrich ended 67 heads over half.

options.label: Heads is now more likely, because the coin is hot
options.rationale: A fair coin cannot get hot; each flip is still 1 in 2.

options.label: Each flip starts fresh; early luck is swamped, not repaid

questions.explanation: Flips are independent, so nothing is due. Over many tries the share of heads settles, because early luck is diluted, not cancelled.

questions.prompt: Why did three dice make 10 more often than 9, though each total comes from six sets of numbers?

options.label: Dice were heavier on the high faces
options.rationale: Fair dice land on each face equally often.

options.label: More of the 216 throws make 10 (27) than 9 (25)
Players rolled 10 on purpose
options.rationale: Galileo explained it with a count, not with cheating.

options.label: Ten is closer to the middle total of 18
options.rationale: The middle of 3 to 18 is 10.5, and the count is what matters.

questions.explanation: Galileo counted throws, not sums: of 216 throws, 27 make 10 and only 25 make 9.

questions.prompt: You roll two dice, then flip a coin. The chance of a total of 7 and then heads is _____.

options.rationale: That treats the 7 as 1 in 4; it is 1 in 6.
That is the chance of double 6 alone.
Adding 1/6 and 1/2 gives 2/3, but "both" must be smaller.

questions.explanation: A 7 is 1 in 6; heads is 1 in 2. The events are independent, so multiply: 1/6 × 1/2 = 1/12.

questions.prompt: Kerrich got 5,067 heads in 10,000 tosses, 67 over an even 5,000. What does that show about the law of large numbers?

options.label: The coin must have been unfair
options.rationale: 50.7% after 10,000 tosses is what a fair coin can easily give.

options.label: The law failed on a real coin
options.rationale: It worked: the share landed close to half.

options.label: The count will even out if you keep going
options.rationale: The count need not even out; only the share settles.

options.label: The share settles near half even when the count is off

questions.explanation: The law promises the share, not the count: 50.7% is close to half, while the gap in the count need not shrink.
